comparisons.peer_topic: Goodwill Impairment Testing Methodology and Results
comparisons.peer_summary: The Corporation performs qualitative assessments to determine if fair value is likely below carrying value, with an option to bypass this and proceed directly to quantitative testing; if quantitative tests show carrying value exceeds fair value, an impairment loss is recognized for the excess of allocated equity over fair value, limited to the assigned goodwill amount, with no subsequent reversals permitted.
comparisons.comparison: Both GS and BAC performed annual goodwill impairment assessments for fiscal 2024 and concluded that goodwill was not impaired because the estimated fair value of each reporting unit exceeded its carrying value. While GS explicitly stated that a quantitative test was not required based on this outcome, BAC’s disclosure outlines the methodology where such a conclusion (fair value > carrying value) results in no impairment recognition, noting they have an option to bypass qualitative assessments to proceed to quantitative tests if needed, though the end result for both was a non-impaired status based on fair value superiority.

sentences.text: As a result of the annual assessment, the firm determined that it was more likely than not that the estimated fair value of each reporting unit with goodwill exceeded its respective carrying value.
Therefore, the firm determined that goodwill for each reporting unit was not impaired and that a quantitative goodwill test was not required.
When performing the quantitative assessment, if the fair value of the reporting unit exceeds its carrying value, goodwill of the reporting unit would not be considered impaired.

comparisons.peer_summary: The quantitative test compares the fair value of a reporting unit to its carrying value, including goodwill. If fair value exceeds carrying value, no impairment is recognized; if carrying value exceeds fair value, an impairment loss is recognized equal to the excess, limited to the total goodwill allocated to that unit.
comparisons.comparison: Both GS and C describe the specific criterion for non-impairment: if the fair value of a reporting unit exceeds its carrying value, goodwill is considered not impaired. GS reports that this condition was met for all reporting units, allowing them to conclude no impairment and skip further quantitative testing. C defines this same outcome in its policy description, stating that if fair value exceeds carrying value, no impairment is recognized and no further analysis is necessary. Both entities effectively used the 'fair value > carrying value' benchmark to confirm the absence of impairment for their reporting units.

comparisons.peer_topic: Goodwill and Indefinite-Lived Intangible Assets Impairment Testing Methodology
comparisons.peer_summary: The Firm tests goodwill and indefinite-lived intangible assets for impairment annually and on an interim basis when events occur. For goodwill, testing is performed at the reporting unit level, while indefinite-lived intangible assets are tested at the aggregate level of management contracts. The Firm may use a qualitative assessment or a quantitative test; if quantitative, impairment is recognized if fair value is less than carrying amount, limited to the asset's carrying amount.
comparisons.comparison: Both GS and MS disclose the methodology and options for goodwill impairment testing, specifically the ability to use a qualitative assessment or proceed to a quantitative test. GS’s disclosure implies the completion of an assessment that resulted in a conclusion of no impairment (fair value > carrying value), consistent with the outcome of a successful qualitative test or a quantitative test showing sufficient fair value. MS details the explicit option to perform a qualitative assessment to determine if quantitative testing is necessary, and if a quantitative test is performed, non-impairment is recognized if fair value is not less than carrying amount. Both reflect the industry standard that fair value superiority over carrying value prevents impairment recognition.

sentences.text: Therefore, the firm determined that goodwill for each reporting unit was not impaired and that a quantitative goodwill test was not required.
When performing a quantitative impairment test of goodwill, the Firm compares the fair value of the reporting unit with the carrying amount.

For both the annual and interim tests, the Firm has the option to either (i) perform a quantitative impairment test or (ii) first perform a qualitative assessment to determine whether it is more likely than not that the fair value is less than its carrying amount, in which case, the quantitative test would be performed.
